title: Food and hosting
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: tafaḍḍal hands something over, invites someone in, offers a seat, gives permission and says "after you". Five English acts, one Arabic word, and it is the most useful thing in the module.
Ordering needs nothing new: urīd from M1 of the level below, min faḍlika from M8, hal turīd from M2 and M3. Only the food is new, which is what makes the module cheap and the vocabulary worth it.

In Arab hosting an offer is EXPECTED to be repeated, so a single lā shukran is heard as politeness rather than as a decision. The refusal that lands adds a reason: lā shukran, anā shabʿān. A host who accepts the first refusal has under-hosted.
shabʿān is an adjective and agrees with the speaker: shabʿān from a man, shabʿāna from a woman — the same law as āsif in M1.
alḥamdu lillāh is what a guest says when the meal ends. It travels as one phrase and neither half of it is used apart in this course.

words.note: Hands something over, invites someone in, offers a seat, gives permission, says after you. Five English acts and one Arabic word; the feminine is tafaḍḍalī.

sentences.trap: It has no single English translation and looking for one wastes the word. Learn it as a gesture: it means "go ahead, it is yours".

sentences.cue: I'd like meat and rice, please
sentences.literal: I-want meat and rice, from your-favour

words.note: Masculine, and bare here because you are naming a kind rather than pointing at a portion. With al- it becomes the meat in front of you.
The r is doubled and held. r is a sun letter, so al- assimilates: ar-ruzz.

sentences.trap: No article on either noun. Naming a kind of food leaves al- off, exactly as L1-M3's urīd shāy did.
sentences.sound: LAḤM, one syllable with the ḥ deep in the throat. RUZZ, with the z held long.

words.note: An adjective, so it agrees with the SPEAKER: shabʿāna from a woman. The ʿayn in the middle is a letter, and the word is unsayable without it.

words.note: The plate and what is on it alike. ṭ is a sun letter and emphatic, so al- assimilates and the ṭ is held long: aṭ-ṭabaq.

words.note: Two words travelling as one, and neither half is used apart in this course. It answers "how are you", ends a meal, and marks any small relief.
